meta.title: Why the Driver Must Know the Car
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses second person.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 127w at FK 5.7, part_2 137w at FK 7.1, part_3 141w at FK 7.7. The load is second person, rhetorical questions, fear appeal, and repetition of 'owner'.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from H. Clifford Brokaw and Charles A. Starr, Putnam's Automobile Handbook (1918), under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Brokaw, H. Clifford, and Charles A. Starr. Putnam's Automobile Handbook: The Care and Management of the Modern Motor-Car. 1918. Project Gutenberg eBook #65673, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/65673, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: Split long sentences, replaced rare words, dropped asides; no facts added.
source.survey: Two driving instructors warn owners that a neglected car can hurt the people riding in it.
source.avoided: No invented crash, injury, or repair detail.

session.difficulty_basis: second person, rhetorical questions, fear appeal, and repetition of 'owner'

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: Few of you would trust your body to wind and waves if you did not believe a good captain and engineer were on board. You would not trust a train without an engineer and conductor to keep you safe. Why should you put yourself and loved ones in a motor car with an unsure hand at the wheel? No one on board can run the engine or know if the parts are set right. A bad setting may mean danger and even death. You would not feel sorry for the owner in an accident caused by ignorance. But the fate of others in his care calls for a warning. A bad brake or a broken part—broken because it was neglected—may be the fool-killer's weapon.
passage.part_2: Even though the owner can afford a chauffeur who “knows all about an auto,” chauffeurs forget. They loaf on the job. They plot with the supply dealer to push upkeep costs sky-high. They have as many road troubles as the common owner. The owner who knows can spot these mistakes, for his comfort and the safety of his bank balance. So now, after you turn to the maker’s instructions and think over the warnings here, you may safely go on to the chapters about the beast you must tame. Yet today there are automobile schools and service stations. No one needs to be ignorant. No one needs to come under the same wise one’s condemnation: “The careless ease of fools shall destroy them.” Give me a person of average intelligence in overalls and jumper.
passage.part_3: Some can be taught to "make the auto auto as it really ought to auto." The chief obstacle is the half knowledge—half error—which some possess. Josh Billings once said: “I’d rather not know so much than know a lot that is not so.” The reader will get the idea. One of the hardest things for the average man to learn is not to do useless things. Over and over folks will do things contrary to all rules and instructions and make extra work for themselves. In a school it is a good thing: it lets the instructor point out how useless it is to go at the thing wrong end first. They were set to locating engine troubles, forgot the rules. Took turns cranking the engine, expecting that way to find out why the engine would not run.

items.prompt: What does the author say a bad setting may mean?

tutor_only.confirm: A bad setting may mean danger and even death.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'A bad setting may mean danger and even death' states the fact.
tutor_only.tell: The author warns that a bad setting may cause danger and death. This warning is a stated fact early in the passage.
help: Look at the sentence after the owner warning.
Find the words about a bad setting and its result.
tutor_only.core_idea: A bad setting may cause danger and death.
accept_ideas: a bad setting can be deadly
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say a bad setting only causes delay.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence names danger and death?

items.prompt: No one on board can run the engine or know if parts are set right. How does that make the warning stronger?

tutor_only.confirm: It shows no one aboard can run the engine or check the parts, so danger can go unseen.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'No one on board can run the engine or know if the parts are set right' gives the two limits that make the warning stronger.
tutor_only.tell: The sentence lists two limits: running the engine and checking the parts. Those limits make the warning about danger feel more real.
help: Look at the sentence about what no one on board can do.
Ask what those two limits mean for the reader's safety.
tutor_only.core_idea: The two limits make the warning stronger because no one aboard can prevent a bad setting.
accept_ideas: No one on board can run the engine or know if parts are set right.
The reader cannot rely on anyone aboard to prevent a bad setting.
The warning is stronger because danger can go unseen.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the writer means the owner can run the engine.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says no one on board can run the engine?

items.prompt: The author says chauffeurs forget and loaf. What should an owner conclude about hiring one?

tutor_only.confirm: An owner should learn enough to catch a chauffeur’s mistakes.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'The owner who knows can spot these mistakes, for his comfort and the safety of his bank balance' supports this conclusion.
tutor_only.tell: Hiring a chauffeur does not remove the owner's need to learn. The passage says an informed owner can spot mistakes.
help: Look at the sentence about the owner who knows.
Ask what knowing lets the owner do about chauffeur mistakes.
tutor_only.core_idea: Hiring help does not remove an owner's need to understand the car and check for mistakes.
accept_ideas: An owner should learn enough to catch a chauffeur's mistakes.
Hiring a chauffeur does not mean the owner can stay ignorant.
The owner needs knowledge to protect comfort and money.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The owner should never hire a chauffeur.
if_they_say.ask: Does the passage forbid hiring chauffeurs, or warn that owners must check them?

if_they_say.when: The owner should trust the chauffeur's expert knowledge.
if_they_say.ask: What does the author say chauffeurs do that an informed owner can spot?

items.prompt: Why does the author repeat the word 'owner'?

tutor_only.confirm: The repeated word is 'owner.' It points to the person responsible for knowing the car.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'The owner who knows can spot these mistakes, for his comfort and the safety of his bank balance' shows the repeated word ties responsibility to the owner's knowledge.
tutor_only.tell: The word 'owner' appears more than once. It keeps the reader focused on the person responsible for the car.
help: Look at the sentence that begins 'The owner who knows...' in the middle of the passage.
Ask who must spot mistakes and keep the car safe.
tutor_only.core_idea: Repeating 'owner' stresses that the car owner is responsible for knowing the car and catching mistakes.
accept_ideas: The owner is responsible for knowing the car.
The owner's knowledge protects his comfort and money.
The owner is the one who must act.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The student says the repetition shows chauffeurs are bad.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says the owner who knows can spot mistakes?

if_they_say.when: The student says the repetition means all owners are rich.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence ties the owner to knowing and spotting mistakes?

if_they_say.when: The student says the repetition warns about accidents.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence connects the owner to spotting mistakes?

items.prompt: Which sentence near the end best shows the author's plan changing from warning to teaching?

tutor_only.confirm: The 'In a school it is a good thing' sentence names an instructor and a lesson. It shows the plan has shifted to teaching.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'In a school it is a good thing: it lets the instructor point out how useless it is to go at the thing wrong end first.' names an instructor and a lesson, showing the plan has shifted to teaching.
tutor_only.tell: The opening warns and scares. The last part shows a lesson with an instructor.
help: Reread the last part for words about school or an instructor.
Compare that with the opening, where the author asks why you would risk a motor car.
tutor_only.core_idea: The author shifts from warning readers about danger to teaching them through a school example.
accept_ideas: The author moves from warning about danger to showing a school lesson.
Part_3 uses an instructor to point out useless mistakes.
The approach changes from fear about accidents to correcting half knowledge.
not_required: A full list of part_1 warnings
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say part_3 still only warns readers.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence near the end names an instructor or a lesson?

if_they_say.when: They choose the Josh Billings quotation as the change.
if_they_say.ask: Does that sentence name teaching or only quote a saying?
